text:
Seeking roots for wings

his forehead

shifts

to the right

and left.


And over the whirlpool

of his face

it fixes itself,

a curtain of the beyond,

curved and broad.


A creature

screams in his nose,

which tries to crush it,

enraged…


A Greek bursts forth

through his distant eyes.


A Greek

whom the Andalusian hills

of his cheekbones

and the trembling valley

of his mouth

smother in vines.


His throat leaps

outward

begging

for the moon-shaped razor

of sharp waters.


Cut it off.

From north to south.

From east to west.


Let the head fly,

the head alone,

wounded by black

sea waves…


And by satyr conches

that fall upon it

like bellflowers

on the face

of an ancient mask.


Silence

his wooden voice,

hollow,

wrapped up

in the nasal catacombs.


Free him from it,

and from its sweet arms,

and from its earthen body.


Only force on him,

before hurling him

into space,

the arch of his eyebrows

until you make them bridges

over the Atlantic,

over the Pacific…


Across which his eyes,

lost ships,

may travel

without ports

or shores…

translation.title: Seeking Roots for Wings...
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem's fractured visual syntax, person shifts, anatomical surrealism, and abrupt imperatives. “Cortádsela” is rendered as the direct command “Cut it off,” without resolving the source's unusual object reference.
